summary: Specifies how GMPLS extensions are encoded in the OSPF routing protocol. It is a standards-track document that complements the general GMPLS routing document.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo is the exact spelling guide for new fields in OSPF messages that carry optical-network road information.

questions: what is ospf te lsa for gmpls
what is the shared risk link group sub-tlv
what is the interface switching capability descriptor
what is a link local opaque lsa
subtitle: The exact OSPF fields that let routers advertise optical and other non-packet links for GMPLS.

tldr.problem: GMPLS needs routers to learn about links that are not ordinary packet links, such as unnumbered links, links with protection, shared failure risk and different switching types. OSPF's traffic engineering advertisements could not describe these.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds four sub-TLVs to the TE Link TLV (types 11, 14, 15 and 16) and defines a link-local TE LSA that lets two neighbors swap link identifiers.
tldr.outcome: It gives implementers the byte-level encoding for the GMPLS routing requirements. It updates RFC 3630 and has itself been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002 and RFC 7074.

facts.label: TE Link Local LSA
facts.value: Opaque LSA type 9, Opaque Type 1, Opaque ID 0

facts.label: Bandwidth units
facts.value: Bytes per second, IEEE floating point

today: RFC 4203 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 3630 and has itself been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002 and RFC 7074.

sections.title: Introduction and the New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
RFC 4203 specifies how to carry link state information for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) in the OSPF routing protocol. The set of enhancements OSPF needs is outlined in a companion document, RFC 4202. This RFC supplies the encoding.

OSPF already advertises traffic engineering (TE) properties in a TE LSA, which is an opaque LSA with area flooding scope. That LSA has a single top-level TLV (Router Address, value 1, or Link, value 2) with nested sub-TLVs. This RFC adds four sub-TLVs to the Link TLV.

  • 11, Link Local/Remote Identifiers, length 8
  • 14, Link Protection Type, length 4
  • 15, Interface Switching Capability Descriptor, variable length
  • 16, Shared Risk Link Group, variable length
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF already lets routers share a map of the network. This memo adds four new kinds of sticky note that routers can attach to a link on that map.

sections.title: Link Local/Remote Identifiers
sections.content:
Sub-TLV type 11 is eight octets long. It holds a four-octet Link Local Identifier followed by a four-octet Link Remote Identifier, which is how a link without its own IP address (an unnumbered link) is named. If the remote identifier is not known yet, it is set to 0.

A node can tell its neighbor its own Link Local Identifier by using a link local Opaque LSA, described in the section on exchanging link local TE information below.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end of a road gives it a nickname. This note carries both nicknames, and if one end has not told the other yet, it writes zero.

sections.title: Link Protection Type and SRLG
sections.content:
The Link Protection Type sub-TLV (type 14, four octets) starts with one octet that is a bit vector of the link's protection capabilities: 0x01 Extra Traffic, 0x02 Unprotected, 0x04 Shared, 0x08 Dedicated 1:1, 0x10 Dedicated 1+1 and 0x20 Enhanced. The values 0x40 and 0x80 are reserved. The other three octets SHOULD be zero when sent and SHOULD be ignored on receipt. The sub-TLV may occur at most once in the Link TLV.

The Shared Risk Link Group sub-TLV (type 16) carries an unordered list of 32-bit numbers, one for each SRLG the link belongs to. Its length is the length of that list in octets. It also may occur at most once in the Link TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: One note says how a road is backed up if it breaks. Another lists which roads would all break together, for example because they cross the same bridge.

sections.title: Interface Switching Capability Descriptor
sections.content:
Sub-TLV type 15 describes what kind of switching an interface can do. It begins with a one-octet Switching Capability, a one-octet Encoding (one of the values in Section 3.1.1 of RFC 3471) and two reserved octets. Then come eight 4-octet Maximum LSP Bandwidth fields, for priority 0 first through priority 7 last, in IEEE floating point format. The units are bytes, not bits, per second.

What follows depends on the Switching Capability value. For the packet types PSC-1 to PSC-4 it is a Minimum LSP Bandwidth, a 2-octet Interface MTU and 2 octets of padding. For TDM it is a Minimum LSP Bandwidth, a one-octet indication (0 for Standard SONET/SDH, 1 for Arbitrary SONET/SDH) and 3 octets of padding. For L2SC and LSC there is no extra information. The padding keeps the sub-TLV 32-bit aligned and SHOULD be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.

An interface with more than one switching capability may have more than one of these sub-TLVs in the Link TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: This note says what the road can carry, from small packets to whole beams of light, and how much of it is free at each priority level.

sections.title: Graceful Restart
sections.content:
A restarting node follows the OSPF restart procedures of RFC 3623 and the RSVP-TE restart procedures of RFC 3473. While it is still working out how much bandwidth is free after the restart, it should originate its Link TLV TE LSAs with 0 unreserved bandwidth and a TE metric of 0xffffffff. If the link's Switching Capability is LSC or FSC, it should also use 0 as the Max LSP Bandwidth.

Before a planned restart, the node SHOULD advertise 0 unreserved bandwidth (and 0 Max LSP Bandwidth for LSC or FSC links), which discourages new LSP setup through it. Its neighbors keep advertising the real unreserved bandwidth on their links toward it. A regular graceful restart should not be aborted when a TE LSA or the TE topology changes.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router reboots, it tells everyone its roads are full until it has checked, so no new traffic is sent its way by mistake.

sections.title: Exchanging Link Local TE Information
sections.content:
Sometimes a node needs to tell only the neighbor on one interface about TE information. If X and Y share an unnumbered point-to-point interface I, X's Link Local Identifier for I is Y's Link Remote Identifier for I. X sends its identifier in a TE Link Local LSA, which is an opaque LSA of type 9 (link-local flooding scope) with Opaque Type 1 and Opaque ID 0.

The body uses the usual TE TLV format: a 2-octet type and a 2-octet length, with the value zero-padded to a four-octet boundary. The top-level type for the Link Local TLV is 4. The only TLV defined is the Link Local Identifier TLV, type 1, length 4, holding the 32-bit Link Local Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Some secrets are only for the neighbor across one road. This is a private note that is passed across that road and goes no further.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions live in Opaque LSAs in OSPFv2. Opaque LSAs are not used for SPF computation or normal routing, so they have no direct effect on IP routing. Tampering with GMPLS TE LSAs may, however, affect the underlying optical or SONET-SDH transport network.

The RFC points to RFC 3630, which suggests mechanisms such as OSPF with digital signatures (RFC 2154), and says these or other mechanisms should be used to secure and authenticate the information.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody should be able to scribble on the map, because a wrong note could send real light beams down the wrong fibers.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The memo introduces four new sub-TLVs of the TE Link TLV. RFC 3630 says sub-TLVs in the range 10 to 32767 are assigned by Expert Review and must be registered with IANA. The RFC strongly recommends that the suggested values (11, 14, 15 and 16) be granted, because there are interoperable implementations using them.

A new top-level type for the Link Local TLV has been allocated from the Standards Action space.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note types need official numbers so that everyone uses the same ones.

fields.name: Link Local Identifier
fields.desc: The sender's identifier for the link.

fields.name: Link Remote Identifier
fields.desc: The neighbor's identifier for the link; 0 if unknown.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: SHOULD be zero when sent, ignored on receipt.
